editor_spans.body: The Derby announcement is mostly about a building, not the trains. GBR's headquarters will hold up to 450 staff and will not be finished until spring 2029. The publicly owned railway is meant to be running well before it has a home, so the real test of 'passengers before profit' is not taking place in Becketwell.

The more revealing number is buried further down: fewer than 7% of railway workers are under 25. Up to 600 apprentices over four years works out at about 150 a year. Against an industry that leans heavily on people nearing retirement, that is a gesture, not a pipeline. The demographic gap built up over decades in which fragmented franchises had little reason to train for the long term. Public ownership removes that excuse. Ministers should be judged on whether apprentice numbers grow well past this opening figure.

The fare freeze and the 76,000 extra seats are real, but they are short-term dividends. Running a railway is the slow, unglamorous work of maintenance, workforce and rolling-stock planning. Ribbon-cuttings in Derby should not be mistaken for it.

Read in order, the week's Ukraine statements show how little of the diplomatic initiative belongs to London. On 9 October the government backed 'US-led efforts' after a US-Russia agreement. By 12 October the Prime Minister was welcoming President Trump's reciprocal energy ceasefire. Two days later he was describing Russian attacks on civilians and energy infrastructure since that call. Britain is reacting to a process it does not control.

The government is candid about one motive: getting diesel back onto world markets, and the effect of the conflicts on prices and the cost of living. That is not cynical, but it matters. British support is now partly tied to energy prices at home, and that link will be tested if a ceasefire comes at Ukraine's expense.

The material commitments are smaller than the rhetoric. 'Doubling down' amounts to accelerating £10 million of a £45 million missile delivery, while the further sanctions, military and fiscal packages are still being 'drawn up'. Britain's real long-term lever is its dominance in shipping and insurance services. That makes the LNG maritime services ban, and persuading partners to copy it, more important than any single missile tranche.

The Commons statement quietly reopens the question British politics has avoided for a decade. The Brussels summit offers a food-and-drink deal, emissions-trading links and a youth scheme. Beyond that, the Prime Minister wants a 'serious dialogue about the different options' for the long-term relationship with the EU.

The border examples, such as 100% document checks on Scottish salmon, banned seed potatoes and £200 certificates, describe costs that were predictable from the form of exit chosen in 2020. The promised gain of over £10 billion a year by 2040 is modest and slow. That is precisely why the government is hinting at going further.

Promising that 'the public will be the boss' and 'complete transparency' is the right instinct. But the claim that public opinion 'currently supports' this approach is the kind of assertion that has gone wrong before. If the long-term relationship really is on the table, ministers should say so plainly before the summit, not after.

The Prime Minister's offer to Holyrood is an unusual piece of politics. Westminster is lecturing a devolved government about over-centralisation, in an area where it has little power to compel anything. Andy Burnham is exporting the city-region model he knows from Manchester, through 'No10 North' and the Scotland Office.

The argument has merit: Scottish local government has long been weak by European standards. But an offer routed through UK ministries will look to Edinburgh like an attempt to build a direct relationship with Scottish regions over the Scottish Government's head. Whether the offer is 'genuine' will be shown by whether it carries money and statutory powers, not by the speeches.
